h: Divine Judgment Awakens Shame and Repentance

p: בְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ שָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁרַבֵּנוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה אָמַר רֶמֶז בְּרָאשֵׁי תֵבוֹת וַיִּגַּשׁ עַל בְּכִיָּה וּצְעָקָה וּבְוַדַּאי יֵשׁ לוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ בַּפָּרָשָׁה.

— Concerning this portion, I heard that our holy teacher, of blessed and holy memory, gave an allusion in the initial letters of Vayigash to weeping and crying out. This certainly has a root in the portion.

וְהָעִנְיָן דְּאִיתָא (בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה צג) רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אוֹמֵר אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַדִּין אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַתּוֹכֵחָה וּמַה יוֹסֵף וְכוּלֵּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁהוּא דַּיָּין וּבַעַל דִּין וְיוֹשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא דִין וְדָן כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה וְכוּלֵּי

— The explanation follows Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 93: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says, Woe to us from the day of judgment! Woe to us from the day of rebuke! If Joseph, etc., then how much more so the Holy One, blessed be He, who is both judge and litigant, sits upon the throne of judgment, and judges each individual, etc.
וְזֶה שֶׁרָמַז שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִצְעוֹק אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַדִּין.
— This is his allusion to the need to cry out: Woe to us from the day of judgment!
וּבַגְּמָרָא (חֲגִיגָה ד:) אִיתָא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא בָּכֵי וְלֹא יָכְלוּ אֶחָיו וְגוֹמֵר וּמַה וְכוּלֵּי וְזֶה שֶׁרָמַז בְּכִיָּה.
— It is taught in the Talmud (Chagigah 4b): When Rabbi Elazar reached this verse, ‘His brothers could not,’ etc., he wept: If, etc. This is the allusion to weeping.
וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה שֶׁהָיָה עֲשִׂירִי לְעֶזְרָא וְאִתְרְחִישׁ לֵיהּ נִיסָא וְאַהְדְּרוּ לֵיהּ תַּמְנֵי סְרֵי דָּרֵי חִיוְּרָתָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת כח.) אָמַר כֵּן.
— Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, a tenth-generation descendant of Ezra, for whom a miracle occurred and eighteen rows of white hair appeared (Berakhot 28a), said this.
מִזֶּה יָכוֹל כָּל אָדָם לָדוּן קַל וָחֹמֶר בְּעַצְמוֹ וְלִצְעוֹק מָרָה אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַדִּין אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַתּוֹכֵחָה.
— From this, each person can apply the inference to himself and cry out bitterly: Woe to us from the day of judgment! Woe to us from the day of rebuke!

וּבְתַנְחוּמָא הַלָּשׁוֹן וּמַה יוֹסֵף וְכוּלֵּי כְּשֶׁעוֹמֵד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַדִּין דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ וּמִי הָעוֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בּוֹ כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי הָאָדָם וָחָי עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה

— Tanchuma's wording is: If Joseph, etc., then when the Holy One, blessed be He, stands in judgment—of whom it is written, ‘Who can endure the day of His coming, and who can stand when He appears?’ and, ‘A person cannot see Me and live’—how much more so!

h: Living Before the King of Kings

p: וְהַיְינוּ עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵישׁ הַגָּהַת אֹרַח חַיִּים) כְּשֶׁיָּשִׂים הָאָדָם אֶל לִבּוֹ שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו מִיָּד יַגִּיעַ אֵלָיו הַיִּרְאָה וְהַפַּחַד וְכוּלֵּי וּבוֹשְׁתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד.

— This accords with the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chayim: When a person takes to heart that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, stands over him and sees his actions, reverence and dread immediately come upon him, etc., and he remains constantly ashamed before Him.

וְהוּא דְּמָצִינוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (שָׁם עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁיְּהֵא מוֹרָא שָׁמַיִם עֲלֵיכֶם כְּמוֹרָא בָּשָׂר וָדָם אָמְרוּ לוֹ תַלְמִידָיו עַד כָּאן אָמַר לָהֶם וּלְוַאי תֵּדְעוּ כְּשֶׁאָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אוֹמֵר שֶׁלֹּא יִרְאַנִי אָדָם.

— We find in the Talmud (ibid., 28b): May the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood. His disciples asked: Only so far? He told them: If only! Know that when a person transgresses, he says, ‘May no person see me.’

וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁזֶּה גַּם כֵּן מַדְרֵגָה בְּיִרְאָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מוֹרָא מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים כְּמוֹרָא בָּשָׂר וָדָם מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּשָׂר וָדָם נִרְאֶה לָעַיִן וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא רוֹאֶה וְאֵינוֹ נִרְאֶה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם י.)

— Thus this too is a level of reverence: fearing the King of kings as one fears flesh and blood. A mortal is visible to the eye, whereas the Holy One, blessed be He, sees but is not seen (ibid., 10a).
וְרַק עַל יְדֵי אֱמוּנָה יָשִׂים הָאָדָם אֶל לִבּוֹ שֶׁעוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו.
— Only through faith does a person take to heart that He stands over him and sees his actions.
וְיֵשׁ מַדְרֵגָה יוֹתֵר כְּשֶׁיְּצַיֵּיר עַל יְדֵי אֱמוּנָה שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְאָז יִגְדַּל הַבּוּשָׁה יוֹתֵר וְיוֹתֵר.
— There is a higher level: through faith he pictures the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, standing over him, and his shame then grows ever greater.
וְכָל זֶה בִּבְחִינַת אֱמוּנָה עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא אִיהִי אֱמוּנָה.
— All this is within the aspect of faith, in the sense of Ra'aya Meheimna's statement, ‘She is faith.’

paragraphs.text: Rema, Orach Chayim 1:1: ““I have placed Hashem before me always” is a great principle in Torah and in the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person’s sitting, movements, and affairs when alone in his house are unlike his sitting, movements, and affairs before a great king. Nor are his speech and free expression with his household and relatives like his speech in the king’s presence. How much more so when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, as it says, “Can a person hide in secret places and I not see him? says Hashem.” Immediately fear, submission in awe of Hashem, and continual shame before Him will reach him.”

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 10a: “Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, fills the entire world, so the soul fills the entire body. Just as the Holy One sees but is not seen, so the soul sees but is not seen. Just as the Holy One sustains the whole world, so the soul sustains the whole body. Just as the Holy One is pure, so the soul is pure. Just as the Holy One dwells in the innermost chambers, so the soul dwells in the innermost chambers. Let that which possesses these five qualities come and praise Him who possesses these five qualities.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Mesillat Yesharim, chapter 24: “The kinds of fear are two that are three. The first is very easy to attain, nothing is as easy, and the second is the hardest of all, and its perfection is likewise a very great perfection. There is fear of punishment, which is the first kind, and there is fear of His exaltedness, which is the second kind, of which fear of sin is a part. … The second kind is fear of exaltedness: a person keeps far from sins and does not commit them because of His great glory, blessed be His Name; for how could the heart of a lowly, contemptible creature of flesh and blood dare to do anything against the will of the Creator, blessed and exalted be His Name? This fear is not so easy to attain, for it is born only of knowledge and understanding, of contemplating His exaltedness, blessed be He, and the lowliness of man. … Through it a person is ashamed and trembles when he stands before his Maker to pray or to perform any service; this is the praiseworthy fear for which the pious of all ages were praised. … Concerning this fear Moses our teacher said, ‘So that His fear shall be upon your faces, that you not sin.’”

p: וְיֵשׁ מַדְרֵגָה גָּבוֹהַּ יוֹתֵר כְּשֶׁזּוֹכִין לִהְיוֹת מְפוֹרָשׁ לָעַיִן שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹמֵד עָלָיו
— There is a still higher level: meriting to have it manifest before one's eyes that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, stands over him.
וְלָזֶה אֵין אָדָם זוֹכֶה בְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְהַשִּׂיג הַיִּרְאָה בִּבְחִינַת אֱמֶת.
— A person in this world does not merit this—to apprehend reverence in the aspect of truth.
וְלֹא זָכָה לָזֶה רַק יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה מֶרְכָּבָה לְשֵׁם הֲוָיָ״ה וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב אִיהוּ אֱמֶת.
— Only our father Jacob, peace be upon him, merited it, for he was a vehicle for the Name Havayah. Thus it says, ‘Give truth to Jacob,’ corresponding to the teaching, ‘He is truth.’
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ הַשְּׁבָטִים כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֵין בְּלִבְּךָ אֶלָּא אֶחָד כָּךְ אֵין בְּלִבֵּנוּ אֶלָּא אֶחָד (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב פְּסָחִים נו.)
— To this the tribes said: Just as there is only One in your heart, so there is only One in our hearts (Pesachim 56a).

וְאָמַרְנוּ כַּמָּה פְעָמִים שֶׁהַמְכוּוָּן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי אֱמוּנָה נוּכַל לְהַשִּׂיג אֱמוּנַת הַיִּחוּד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּמְפוֹרָשׁ לְנֶגֶד עַיִן שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ קוֹדֶם בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם.

— We have said many times that through faith we can attain belief in Divine unity until it is as though manifest before our eyes that everything comes from Hashem, as before the creation of the world.
וְהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַשֵּׁם בִּבְחִינַת אֱמֶת. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (נְדָרִים כ.) וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם זוֹ בּוּשָׁה.
— This is apprehending Hashem in the aspect of truth. Thus it is taught (Nedarim 20a), ‘So that His fear shall be upon your faces’ refers to shame.
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שֶׁאָז נִגְלָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְעֵין כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר פָּנִים בְּפָנִים דִּיבֶּר הַשֵּׁם עִמָּכֶם וְגוֹמֵר
— Because Hashem then revealed Himself before the eyes of all Israel, as it is said, ‘Face to face Hashem spoke with you,’ etc.,

נִשְׁאַר מִזֶּה לְדוֹרוֹת עוֹלָם שֶׁיּוּכַל הָאָדָם לְצַיֵּיר בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו שֶׁעַל יְדֵי כֵן יַגִּיעֵהוּ הַפַּחַד וּבָשְׁתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד.

— there remains for all generations the ability to picture in one's heart the King of kings standing over him and seeing his actions. Through this, dread reaches him, and he is constantly ashamed before Him.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ תַלְמִידֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר עַד כָּאן שֶׁמְּבָרְכָם רַק בְּצִיּוּר שֶׁעוֹמֵד עָלָיו בָּשָׂר וָדָם וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו
— This was the disciples of Rabbi Eliezer's question, ‘Only so far?’ He blessed them only with envisioning a mortal standing over them and seeing their actions.
הָא יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגָה יוֹתֵר שֶׁיְּצַיֵּיר הָאָדָם בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו
— But there is a higher level: envisioning in one's heart the King of kings standing over him and seeing his actions.
וְעַל זֶה הֱשִׁיבָם שֶׁגַּם זֶה מַדְרֵגָה בְּיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁעַל כָּל פָּנִים מוֹנַעְתּוֹ מִלַּחֲטוֹא
— He answered that this too is a level of fear of Heaven, since it at least prevents him from sinning.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (שָׁם) שֶׁכָּל אָדָם הַמִּתְבַּיֵּישׁ לֹא בִמְהֵרָה הוּא חוֹטֵא וּמִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ בוֹשֶׁת פָּנִים בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁלֹּא עָמְדוּ אֲבוֹתָיו עַל הַר סִינַי.
— Concerning this they said there: Anyone who feels shame will not readily sin; one who lacks shame is known not to have had ancestors who stood at Mount Sinai.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shoftim 6: “The Talmud (Nedarim 20a) expounds the verse, ‘So that His fear shall be upon your faces’: this is shame; ‘that you not sin’: this teaches that shame leads to fear of sin. It is like the fear of flesh and blood, as taught (Berakhot 28a): Know that when a person commits a transgression he says, ‘May no person see me,’ for he is ashamed before him. So too, when a person pictures to himself that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, stands over him and sees his deeds, even though he does not actually see this before his eyes, yet when he pictures it through faith, believing that the King of kings stands over him, at once fear and submission from the dread of Hashem come upon him, and he is constantly ashamed before Him (as in the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chayim). This is ‘fearing shame.’ It was for this that the stand at Mount Sinai availed, as it says there, ‘So that His fear shall be upon your faces’: every Jew believes that the King of kings stands over him, and can picture it as though he saw it with his senses, like the fear of flesh and blood. This is what the Mishnah says (Avot 5), ‘The shamefaced to the Garden of Eden’: if he only has shame, he is already prepared for the Garden of Eden, for he will surely have fear of the dread of Hashem and will not sin.”

h: Preparing Now for the Future Reckoning

p: וְלֶעָתִיד שֶׁהַכֹּל יִרְאוּ עַיִן בְּעַיִן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹאֶה כָל מַעֲשֵׂי בְּנֵי אָדָם
— In the future, when everyone sees directly that Hashem sees all human deeds,
אָז יֵבוֹשׁ הָאָדָם בְּמַעֲשָׂיו כְּעִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹשְׁתִּי וְנִכְלַמְתִּי לְהָרִים אֱלֹהַי פָּנַי אֵלֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר
— a person will then be ashamed of his deeds, in the sense of ‘I am ashamed and humiliated to lift my face to You, my God,’ etc.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ וּמִי הָעוֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ.
— Thus it says, ‘Who can endure the day of His coming, and who can stand when He appears?’
וְזֶה דִּמְסַיֵּים בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא שֶׁכָּתוּב בּוֹ כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי הָאָדָם וָחָי שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָאָדָם בַּחַיִּים הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹאֶה וְאֵינוֹ נִרְאֶה
— This is why Midrash Tanchuma concludes with ‘A person cannot see Me and live’: as long as a person is alive, Hashem sees but is not seen.
וְלֶעָתִיד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ וְיִרְאוּ הַכֹּל עַיִן בְּעַיִן כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹמֵד עֲלֵיהֶם תָּמִיד תִּגְדַּל הַבּוּשָׁה מְאֹד אַךְ אָז לֹא יוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה.
— In the future, when He appears and everyone sees directly that Hashem constantly stands over them, their shame will be exceedingly great; but then repentance will no longer avail.

אֲשֶׁר עַל כֵּן כָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָאָדָם בַּחַיִּים וְיִתֵּן אֶל לִבּוֹ לְהַשִּׂיג עַל כָּל פָּנִים עַל יְדֵי אֱמוּנָה שֶׁמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְרוֹאֶה בְּמַעֲשָׂיו יִזְכֶּה לְמִדַּת בּוֹשֶׁת פָּנִים וּבָשְׁתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד.

— Therefore, while a person is alive, let him take to heart and apprehend, at least through faith, that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, stands over him and sees his actions. He will merit the quality of shame and constant modesty before Him.
וְזֶה הַלִּימּוּד בְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ מִמַּה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וְלֹא יָכְלוּ אֶחָיו לַעֲנוֹת אוֹתוֹ כִּי נִבְהֲלוּ מִפָּנָיו מִפְּנֵי הַבּוּשָׁה כְּפֵרוּשׁ רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי.
— This is the lesson of the portion from ‘His brothers could not answer him, because they were terrified before his face’—because of shame, as Rashi explains.

וְלָכֵן רָמַז רַבֵּנוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בְּשֵׁם הַפָּרָשָׁה לִצְעוֹק וְלִבְכּוֹת כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה בְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא יָבֹאוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לִידֵי בּוֹשֶׁת פָּנִים בְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּשֶׁלֹּא יוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה.

— Our holy teacher therefore alluded in the portion's name to crying out and weeping, so that people repent in this world and do not, Heaven forbid, come to shame in the World to Come, when repentance no longer avails.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Shaarei Teshuvah, Gate I, §22: “When the sinner sees that God passes over his sin and is patient with him, does not exact payment from him, and has not dealt with him according to his sins or repaid him according to his iniquities, he should increase the shame in his heart. Surely one who sins against a mortal king and betrays him will be ashamed before him when the king forgives him. Thus it is written: “So that you remember and are ashamed of all your deeds, when I forgive you for everything you have done.” Our Sages said that one who does something and is ashamed of it is forgiven for all his sins. … A person attains this degree of shame by withdrawing to contemplate God’s greatness and how great is the evil of rebelling against His word, and by constantly remembering that God sees his deeds, examines his innermost being, and observes his thoughts.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Rabbenu Yonah adds that divine patience and forgiveness can themselves deepen shame before God. His practical instruction—to contemplate God’s greatness and remember His knowledge of one’s deeds and thoughts—develops Rav Tzadok’s call to cultivate this awareness during life, while it can still lead to repentance.

h: Shabbat Opens the Way to Repentance

p: וּבְשַׁבָּת שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ כָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב תַּעֲנִית ח:) וְנַעֲשֶׂה הָאָדָם עָנִי וּנְכֵה רוּחַ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּדְרַשׁ (רֵישׁ סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה) וְאֵי זֶה מְקוֹם מְנוּחָתִי עַל יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת.

— On Shabbat all Israel are called ‘those who fear My Name’ (Ta'anit 8b), and a person becomes poor and contrite in spirit. At the beginning of Seder Eliyahu Rabbah, ‘Where is the place of My rest?’ is interpreted as referring to Shabbat.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה וְהַבּוּשָׁה יָבֹא הָאָדָם לִתְשׁוּבָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּדְרַשׁ (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יט.) יְרֵא הַשֵּׁם שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵּי
— Through reverence and shame a person comes to repentance, as expounded (Avodah Zarah 19a): one ‘who fears Hashem’ is one who repents, etc.

וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּשִׁיר שֶׁל שַׁבָּת טוֹב לְהוֹדוֹת לַהַשֵּׁם עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וּמוֹדֶה וְעוֹזֵב יְרוּחָם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (פִּרְקֵי דְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק יט) שֶׁכָּל מִי שֶׁמּוֹדֶה וְעוֹזֵב נִיצּוֹל מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם.

— Thus the Shabbat psalm says, ‘It is good to acknowledge Hashem,’ corresponding to ‘One who confesses and abandons his sin will receive mercy.’ Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer, chapter 19, teaches that whoever confesses and abandons his sin is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom.
וְכֵן כָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה כב) כָּךְ כֹּחָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה פָּתַח וְאָמַר מִזְמוֹר שִׁיר לְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת טוֹב לְהוֹדוֹת וְגוֹמֵר:
— Likewise, Bereishit Rabbah, end of chapter 22, states: Such is the power of repentance! He began and said, ‘A psalm, a song for the Shabbat day. It is good to acknowledge,’ etc.

paragraphs.text: Seder Eliyahu Rabbah 1: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: Did I not write for you in My Torah, “This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth”? Although you work during all six days, let Shabbat be devoted entirely to Torah. Hence they said: A person should rise early and study on Shabbat, go to the synagogue and house of study, read the Torah and study the Prophets, and afterward go home to eat and drink, fulfilling “Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a good heart.” For the Holy One has rest only with those who practice Torah, as it says, “My hand made all these… But to this one I look: to the poor and broken in spirit, who trembles at My word.””
